concepts.title: Error Propagation: try/catch, Callbacks, Promises, and Async/Await
concepts.description: The same failure surfaces differently depending on which asynchronous pattern you use. try/catch alone can't catch callback-based errors, while Promises and async/await were designed to make catching an error across an asynchronous gap work. Knowing which mechanism applies where is the difference between a handled failure and an undetected one.
learningObjectives: Explain why a try/catch block wrapped around a callback-based async call fails to catch an error thrown inside that callback.
Explain why Node's core APIs pass errors as callback arguments rather than throwing them directly.
Trace how a rejection propagates through a chain of .then() calls to a single .catch(), including a throw inside a .then() handler.
Use try/catch with async/await to catch a rejected awaited Promise, and identify the bug caused by a missing await inside a try block.
Diagnose why an async function passed as an event handler or route callback can fail silently if its rejection is never awaited or caught by the caller.

sections.heading: Where try/catch Works: The Same Call Stack, While It's Still Alive
Why Callbacks Pass Errors as Data Instead of Throwing
Promises: A Rejection Propagates Through the Chain to a Single catch
async/await: try/catch Works Again, but Only for What You await
The Trap: An async Function Called From Code That Ignores Promises

examples.title: try/catch Failing to Catch an Async Callback Error
examples.explanation: The try block finishes (and the function logs its final message) right after fs.readFile is called, well before the file system operation completes, because fs.readFile is non-blocking and returns at once. By the time the callback runs and throws, the try/catch around the original call has finished and isn't 'listening' for anything; there's no live call stack for the throw to unwind into. The throw propagates up through the Node internals that invoked the callback and becomes an uncaught exception that (as the next concept covers) crashes the process by default, the opposite of what the author intended with the try/catch.

examples.title: A Rejection Propagating Through a Promise Chain
examples.explanation: fetchUser(-1) rejects immediately, and that rejection skips every subsequent .then() in the chain: fetchOrders is never called, the orders.length === 0 check never runs, and the final console.log never executes, so control jumps to the single .catch() at the end. This is what makes Promise chains easier to reason about than nested callbacks: you don't have to ask 'did I check for an error at this step' at every .then(), because a rejection from anywhere earlier reaches the one .catch() that's present, skipping everything in between.

examples.title: Missing await Escaping a try/catch's Protection
examples.explanation: Because chargeCard(orderId) is called without await, processOrder doesn't pause for its result: it continues to the next line and logs the success message whatever chargeCard's Promise does. The try/catch would work if chargeCard were awaited, but nothing here awaits that Promise or attaches a handler to it, so its rejection has no catch block watching for it. It becomes an unhandled rejection a moment later, disconnected from the try/catch that looks, at a glance, as if it should have caught it. This variant of the missing-await bug is dangerous because the code appears to succeed (it logs the success message) while masking a real failure.

misconceptions.description: Wrapping an asynchronous call in try/catch will catch any error related to that call, regardless of whether it's callback-based, Promise-based, or awaited.
misconceptions.clarification: try/catch only catches synchronous throws within its own still-executing call stack and, via await, rejections from Promises you paused on inside the try block. A callback runs later, outside that original call stack, so a throw inside it can't be caught by a try/catch wrapped around the original call, however the code is indented to make it look related. Even with Promises, only a Promise that's awaited (or given a .then/.catch handler) gets its rejection routed to that catch; a Promise-returning call made without await inside a try block produces a Promise the try/catch never looks at again, and a later rejection from it goes unnoticed by that catch.

misconceptions.description: Once a function is declared async, any error occurring anywhere inside it is automatically handled or safe by virtue of the async keyword itself.
misconceptions.clarification: async guarantees only that the function returns a Promise and that a thrown error or a rejected, awaited Promise inside its body becomes a rejection of that returned Promise. It doesn't mean the error is caught anywhere. Something still has to wrap the risky code in a local try/catch, or the caller has to attach a .catch() (or await it inside its own try/catch) to the returned Promise. An async function called by code that does neither, a common trap when passing one to an EventEmitter-based API like http.createServer or socket.on, leaves its rejections unhandled, and nothing async-specific steps in to save it.
misconceptions.fact: async only guarantees that the function returns a Promise, and that a thrown error or a rejected, awaited Promise inside its body becomes a rejection of that returned Promise -- it does not mean the error is caught or handled anywhere.

exercises.prompt: What does this log, and does the catch block ever run? Explain why, referring to which call stack is alive when the error occurs.
hints: setTimeout schedules its callback to run LATER, after the current synchronous code has finished -- has the try block already finished executing by the time that callback actually runs?
Compare this to the fs.readFile example from the explanation. The mechanism is the same, with a timer instead of a file read.
A throw inside a setTimeout callback has nowhere to be caught nearby. Predict what happens to the whole process, not just whether this catch block runs.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'readConfig: scheduled the read' logs, then 'after readConfig() call' logs, then, once the timer fires, the thrown Error becomes an uncaught exception (the catch block never runs), which by default crashes the Node process.
exercises.solutionExplanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) schedules fn to run asynchronously, after all current synchronous code finishes, so readConfig()'s try block runs to completion (logging 'readConfig: scheduled the read') and returns without waiting for the timer. The catch block has no chance to run, since nothing has thrown yet. Control returns to the caller, which logs 'after readConfig() call'. Only later, when the event loop reaches the timers phase and invokes the callback, does throw new Error(...) execute, and by then the try/catch that surrounded the setTimeout call is gone from the call stack (that function call already returned), so no matching catch exists. It becomes an uncaught exception, which by default terminates the process with a stack trace, the same mechanism as the fs.readFile example, triggered by a timer instead of a file read.

exercises.prompt: This Express-style route handler is supposed to catch any failure from fetching a user and respond with a clean 404, but when the lookup fails, the client gets a 200 response with an empty JSON object ({}) and the process then reports an unhandled rejection. Find and fix the bug.
hints: fetchUserById returns a Promise. Is the route handler declared async, and is that Promise awaited anywhere in this code?

A rejection from a Promise that's never awaited (and never given a .then/.catch) isn't caught by a try/catch that merely surrounds it in the source; the try/catch has 'moved on' by the time the rejection happens.
You'll need to mark the handler function async and add await in front of the fetchUserById call so the try/catch actually has something to catch.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original handler calls fetchUserById(req.params.id) without await, so `user` is bound to a Promise object, not the resolved value, and res.json(user) runs immediately. A Promise serializes to {}, so the client gets a 200 with an empty object. When the Promise later rejects, nothing is watching: the surrounding try/catch finished executing when it moved past the Promise-returning line, so it can't catch something that happens afterward. The fix marks the handler async and awaits fetchUserById. Now if the Promise rejects, await re-throws the rejection at that line, and the surrounding try/catch (watching, because the function is paused there) catches it, so the catch block sends the intended 404.

assessments.prompt: Why does wrapping fs.readFile('./file.txt', (err, data) => { if (err) throw err; ... }) in a try/catch fail to catch the thrown error?
options: try/catch only works for errors of type TypeError; a generic Error thrown this way needs a different syntax entirely.
fs.readFile never actually throws errors of any kind, so there's nothing for the catch to catch in the first place.
The catch block's syntax is wrong -- it needs to specify (err) as a parameter matching the callback's err parameter name to work.
The callback runs later, asynchronously, after the try block has already finished executing and its call stack is gone -- there is no live try/catch left for a throw inside the callback to reach.
assessments.explanation: try/catch is tied to the currently executing call stack: a throw is caught only if it happens while the try block's stack frame is still active. fs.readFile returns immediately (it's non-blocking), so the try block finishes and its frame is gone long before the callback runs, and a throw inside that later callback has no matching catch to reach. The “fs.readFile never actually throws errors of any…” option is wrong: the callback in this example does throw, to illustrate the point. The “try/catch only works for errors of type…” option is wrong: try/catch catches any thrown value, not just TypeErrors. The “The catch block's syntax is wrong…” option is wrong: catch parameter names have no matching requirement with any other variable, and this isn't a naming or syntax issue.

assessments.prompt: Inside a .then() handler in a Promise chain, the code executes `throw new Error('No orders found');`. What happens to that throw?
options: It becomes an uncaught exception immediately, crashing the process, since .then() handlers aren't wrapped in any implicit try/catch.
JavaScript automatically catches it and converts it into a resolved value of undefined for the next .then() in the chain.
It's automatically converted into a rejection of the Promise that this specific .then() call itself returns.
It silently terminates the entire chain, with no further callback -- including any .catch() -- ever running again.
assessments.explanation: A synchronous throw inside a .then() callback is caught internally by the Promise machinery and converted into a rejection of the Promise .then() returns, with no special syntax needed. That rejection behaves like any other in the chain, skipping subsequent .then() calls until it reaches a .catch(). The “It becomes an uncaught exception immediately, crashing…” option ignores that Promises catch synchronous throws inside their handlers for this purpose. The “It silently terminates the entire chain…” option is wrong -- a .catch() further down the chain is precisely what does still run. The “JavaScript automatically catches it and converts…” option is wrong -- a throw becomes a rejection, not a silently resolved value.

assessments.prompt: Inside an async function's try block: `const orders = fetchOrders(user.id);` (missing await) is followed by `return summarize(orders);`, still inside the same try. If fetchOrders' Promise later rejects, does the surrounding catch block run?
options: Yes, but only if summarize(orders) itself explicitly checks whether its argument is a Promise before using it.

No -- try/catch only catches a rejection from a Promise that was actually awaited (or otherwise given a handler) inside the try block; since fetchOrders' Promise here was never awaited, its eventual rejection happens completely outside anything the try block is watching, and becomes an unhandled rejection instead.
Yes -- try/catch catches a rejection from any Promise created inside the try block, whether it was awaited or not.
No, because try/catch cannot be used at all inside an async function -- only chained .catch() calls work there.
assessments.explanation: try/catch only catches something the try block is still 'watching' at the moment of failure; for a Promise, that means it was awaited (or given a .then/.catch) inside the try. Since fetchOrders(user.id) is called without await, the try block moves on without pausing; when that Promise rejects, the try/catch has finished its body and nothing catches the rejection, so it becomes an unhandled rejection. The “Yes -- try/catch catches a rejection…” option describes Promise auto-catching that doesn't exist. The “Yes, but only if summarize(orders) itself explicitly…” option is irrelevant: summarize receiving a Promise instead of data is a separate problem from whether the rejection gets caught. The “No, because try/catch cannot be used…” option is wrong: try/catch works inside async functions, for awaited Promises.

assessments.prompt: An async function is passed directly as the request handler to http.createServer. Inside it, `await fetchDataThatMightReject()` is called with no surrounding try/catch anywhere in the handler. If that call rejects, what happens?
options: http.createServer has no concept of Promises at all -- it invokes the handler and moves on, never awaiting or attaching a .catch() to whatever it returns.
The rejection is automatically logged to the console by Node's EventEmitter internals, with no further effect on the request or process.
Because the handler function is declared async, JavaScript guarantees its rejection is caught by the nearest enclosing scope automatically, even without an explicit try/catch.
http.createServer automatically awaits the handler's returned Promise and sends a built-in error response if it rejects.
assessments.explanation: http.createServer (like EventEmitter-based APIs generally) has no awareness that a handler might be async: it calls the function and moves on, never inspecting, awaiting, or attaching a .catch() to the returned Promise. If the awaited call rejects with no local try/catch, the rejection has nowhere to go: it's unhandled, the response is never finished (the client hangs), and on Node 15 and later the process crashes by default. The “http.createServer automatically awaits the handler's returned Promise…” and “The rejection is automatically logged…” options invent automatic handling that Promise-unaware APIs don't provide. The “Because the handler function is declared async…” option is wrong: async only guarantees the function returns a Promise and creates no automatic catching in whatever code calls it.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer asks: 'If try/catch, Promise chains, and async/await are all just different ways of handling errors, why does it matter which one I use for a given piece of code?' Using the async patterns module's coverage of callbacks/Promises/async-await as a starting point, explain why the error-handling mechanism has to match the asynchronous style actually being used.
assessments.modelAnswer: The three asynchronous styles (error-first callbacks, Promises, and async/await) differ in how they deliver a failure that happens after the code that started the operation has finished running, and each needs its own matching mechanism to receive it. Using the wrong one doesn't produce a syntax error; it just fails to catch anything. Plain try/catch is built around the currently executing call stack and can only catch a throw while its own stack frame is alive. An error-first callback always runs later, after the function that scheduled it has returned, so a throw inside it has no live try/catch to reach. That's why Node's core APIs never throw for expected async failures and pass the error as the callback's first argument, which you check with an if statement rather than something a surrounding try/catch could intercept. Promises solve the same problem differently: a rejection skips forward through a chain of .then() calls until it reaches a .catch(), which works because .then()/.catch() are how Promises attach handlers, not because try/catch is involved. async/await re-introduces try/catch, but only for what you await inside the try block: await pauses the function and re-throws a rejection at that line, giving the surrounding try/catch something live to catch. Skip the await on a Promise-returning call and its rejection happens disconnected from the nearby try/catch, because nothing paused to route it there. So you have to use the mechanism that's wired into the style you chose: if (err) checks for callbacks, a chain-ending .catch() for raw Promises, and try/catch around awaited calls for async/await. None of the three bridges into the others automatically, and mixing them up (try/catch around a callback, or a missing await in an async/await try block) produces code that looks like it handles errors while letting them slip through.

concepts.title: Operational vs Programmer Errors, and Why Crashing Can Be Correct
concepts.description: Not every error deserves the same response. An anticipated failure (a network timeout, a missing file, bad user input) should be handled gracefully, while a bug that violates your program's assumptions about its state signals that continuing to run risks operating on corrupted data. Node's uncaughtException/unhandledRejection defaults reflect that distinction.
learningObjectives: Distinguish operational errors (anticipated failure modes of a working system) from programmer errors (bugs that violate the program's own assumptions).
Explain why catching a programmer error and continuing execution is often riskier than letting the process crash.
Explain what process.on('uncaughtException') and process.on('unhandledRejection') are for, and why Node's documentation warns against using them to simply resume normal operation.
Design a custom error type that marks whether a given failure is operational, and use that flag to decide between a graceful response and a controlled crash.
Explain why a process manager or orchestrator restarting a crashed process is a legitimate production strategy, not a fragile workaround.

sections.heading: Two Fundamentally Different Kinds of Errors
sections.body:
The easy approach is to treat every Error the same way (catch it, log it, keep going), but that glosses over a distinction that determines the *correct* response. An **operational error** is a failure a correctly written program can expect during normal operation because the outside world is unreliable: a database connection timing out, a requested file not existing, a downstream API returning a 500, a user submitting invalid input, a network socket getting reset. None of these indicate a bug in your code. They mean the environment didn't behave the way the happy path assumed, and a well-written program anticipates and handles them (retry, fall back, return a 400 to the client, log and move on).

A **programmer error**, by contrast, is a bug: calling a method on something undefined because the code assumed a shape of data that isn't there, an off-by-one that corrupts an array, a violated invariant in your own logic, a TypeError from a value that your own design says should never be null at that point. The difference isn't the JavaScript mechanism that signals either kind (both may show up as a thrown Error or TypeError) but what the error *means*. An operational error says 'the world outside my code didn't cooperate, and I planned for that'; a programmer error says 'my understanding of my program's state at this point was wrong,' which is a different and more worrying problem.

sections.heading: Why 'Just Catch Everything and Keep Going' Is Dangerous for Programmer Errors
sections.body: It's easy to reach for a broad try/catch (or a global uncaughtException handler, covered next) that logs the error and lets the program carry on. For an operational error that's often fine: the failure was anticipated, it's isolated to one operation, and the rest of the program's state is unaffected. For a programmer error it's a riskier bet, because **by the time the error surfaced, you don't know how much damage was done before it did.** A TypeError three lines after some shared, mutable state was updated incorrectly means that state may already be wrong in ways the thrown error doesn't describe or limit. Swallowing the error means continuing to run a program whose internal model has diverged from reality in an unknown way. That's the reasoning behind the sometimes surprising guidance that, for programmer errors, **crashing the process is often the safest response**. Crashing isn't good in itself; continuing in an unknown, possibly corrupted state is worse, and a clean restart (from a process manager, an orchestrator, a container runtime) gets you back to a known-good state more reliably than trying to work out how far the corruption spread.

sections.heading: uncaughtException and unhandledRejection: What They're For
Marking Operational Errors on Purpose
Why Crash-and-Restart Is a Legitimate Strategy, Not a Cop-Out
sections.body: Exiting a process after a programmer error works only in an environment that will restart it, which is why the pattern is common in production Node deployments: process managers like pm2, container orchestrators like Kubernetes, and even a systemd service unit with Restart=on-failure notice that a process exited and bring up a fresh one, without the possibly corrupted in-memory state the crashed process accumulated. This turns 'the process crashed' from an outage into a brief blip for the requests that were in flight, while every other running instance (in a typical multi-process or multi-replica deployment) keeps serving traffic. Trying to build code that never crashes, by swallowing every error including outright bugs, tends to go worse: a process that stays 'up' in name only, accumulating corrupted state and producing increasingly strange, hard-to-diagnose failures, which is a harder incident to detect and recover from than a clean, logged crash and automatic restart. Don't confuse a crash with a planned shutdown: when a deploy or scale-down sends your process SIGTERM, handle it with process.on('SIGTERM', ...), stop accepting connections with server.close(), let in-flight requests finish, and exit with code 0. Exit with a non-zero code only for the failure case, so your supervisor can tell the two apart.

examples.title: AppError: Marking Operational Errors on Purpose
examples.explanation: The throw new AppError('User not found', 404) represents a case the author thought about and decided how to handle: a missing user is a normal outcome of looking one up by an arbitrary id, not evidence that anything is broken. The final line has no such handling. If user.tier is ever undefined (say, because an upstream change to db.findUser dropped that field), .toUpperCase() throws a plain TypeError that nobody marked as operational, because nobody anticipated it. That is the distinction this concept draws between errors you designed for and errors that reveal your code's assumptions were wrong.

examples.title: A Minimal, Correct uncaughtException Handler
examples.explanation: This handler does what Node's documentation recommends and little more: it logs the error for diagnosis, runs a brief cleanup step (server.close(), which stops accepting new connections and lets in-flight ones finish), and then exits. It doesn't try to resume normal operation or keep serving new requests, and it includes a timeout safety net so a slow or stuck close() can't leave the process hanging in a state that should already have exited. (Strictly, the documentation asks for synchronous cleanup; server.close() is asynchronous, which is why the timer guards it, and a stricter handler would skip graceful draining.) The unref() call on the timeout tells Node not to let this pending timer alone keep the process alive if everything else has finished.

examples.title: The Anti-Pattern: Swallowing Everything to 'Stay Up'
examples.explanation: The uncaughtException handler here does the thing Node's documentation warns against: it lets the process resume normal operation after an unanticipated error instead of cleaning up and exiting. The bug, assuming cache[key] is already an array, is a programmer error, and once it throws, this code can't know what else depends on that missing 'scores' update having happened. Continuing to serve requests means every later read from cache operates on a structure that's missing an update, with no error, no crash, and no signal that anything is wrong. That slow, hard-to-trace corruption is what a controlled crash and restart avoids.

misconceptions.description: Adding a process.on('uncaughtException', ...) handler makes an application more robust, since it prevents crashes -- so every production app should have one that logs and continues.
misconceptions.clarification: Node's documentation warns that it is not safe to resume normal operation after an uncaught exception. By definition the error escaped every try/catch in the code, which almost always signals a programmer error whose blast radius (what state was corrupted before the throw) is unknown. The correct, narrow use of the handler is synchronous cleanup and diagnostic logging followed by process.exit(), not swallowing the error to keep the process alive. A process that 'never crashes' because it catches everything, bugs included, tends to accumulate silent corruption that's far harder to detect and debug than a clean, logged crash followed by an automatic restart.

misconceptions.description: Every error should be caught with try/catch somewhere in the code so the program never has to crash.
misconceptions.clarification: This treats 'never crashing' as an unconditional goal, but for programmer errors (bugs that reveal the program's model of its state was wrong) crashing and letting a process manager restart with a clean slate is often safer than catching the error and continuing in an unknown, possibly corrupted state. The goal isn't zero crashes. It's handling anticipated, operational failures gracefully (with explicit error handling, often marked via something like an isOperational flag) while letting unanticipated errors surface loudly enough to be noticed, logged, and recovered from by a restart, not papered over.

exercises.prompt: Given the AppError pattern from this concept, what response (status code and body) does each of these two requests get, assuming the error-handling middleware checks err.isOperational as shown in the explanation?
hints: Request A hits the `if (!product)` check. What kind of error does that branch construct, and is it marked isOperational?
Request B doesn't trigger that check, since product IS found. It fails later, reading .amount off product.price, which is undefined. Is THAT error marked isOperational by anything in this code?
Compare what the error-handling middleware does for an isOperational error versus one with no such flag at all (undefined is falsy).
exercises.expectedAnswer: Request A: 404 with a JSON body like {"error":"Product not found"}, from a deliberately constructed, marked AppError. Request B: a plain TypeError (reading .amount off undefined), NOT marked isOperational, so the middleware treats it as unexpected, responding 500 with a generic error body and (per this concept's pattern) crashing the process for a clean restart.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Request A triggers the if (!product) check, which constructs an AppError('Product not found', 404), with isOperational: true and statusCode: 404 by construction, and passes it to next(). The error middleware recognizes err.isOperational and responds with the anticipated 404 and a clean message. Request B finds a product, so it skips that branch, then reads product.price.amount. Since product.price is undefined for this record, reading .amount throws a plain TypeError, which the surrounding try/catch forwards to next(err) too. But this TypeError was never an AppError, so err.isOperational is undefined, which is falsy. The middleware falls into the 'unexpected error' branch: it logs the error, responds with a generic 500, and, following this concept's pattern, exits the process so a manager can restart with clean state, since a bug like this means the assumption that product records always have a price was wrong.

exercises.prompt: A teammate added this global handler to 'make the server more resilient' after seeing occasional crashes in production logs. Explain what's wrong with this fix and rewrite it to follow the guidance in this concept.
hints: Neither handler calls process.exit(). What does Node's documentation say about resuming normal operation after an uncaughtException?
By the time either handler runs, an error has escaped every try/catch (or .catch()) in the code. Is that more likely an anticipated, operational failure or an unanticipated bug?
The fix isn't MORE suppression. Log with enough detail to diagnose the issue, do any quick synchronous cleanup, and then exit so a process manager can restart cleanly.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original handlers do what Node's documentation warns against: they log a message and let the process resume normal operation, on the assumption that this makes the server 'more resilient.' An error reaching either handler has escaped every try/catch and .catch() in the code, which is the hallmark of an unanticipated programmer error, since operational failures are normally caught and handled where they occur. Continuing afterward risks operating on partially corrupted state, with no way to know how far the corruption spread. The fix logs the error in full (console.error, passing the whole err/reason object rather than just its message, to preserve the stack trace) and then calls process.exit(1), so whatever supervises the process (pm2, Kubernetes, systemd, etc.) can start a fresh instance with known-good state instead of leaving a possibly corrupted process running under the illusion of resilience.

assessments.prompt: According to Node's own documentation and the reasoning behind it, what is the correct thing to do inside a process.on('uncaughtException', handler) callback?
options: Log the error and return normally, so the process keeps running exactly as it did before the exception.
Automatically retry whatever operation caused the exception, up to three times, before giving up.
Nothing needs to be done -- Node automatically restarts the internal event loop after logging the error itself.
Perform any necessary synchronous cleanup (closing resources, flushing logs) and then call process.exit(), since it is not considered safe to resume normal operation after an uncaught exception.
assessments.explanation: Node's documentation says resuming normal operation after an uncaughtException is unsafe, because the exception escaped every try/catch in the code, which usually indicates a programmer error whose impact on the program's state is unknown. The recommended pattern is cleanup then exit: do whatever quick, synchronous cleanup is feasible (closing a server to stop new connections, flushing critical logs) and then exit, relying on a process manager or orchestrator to restart with clean state. The “Log the error and return normally…” option is the anti-pattern this concept warns against. The “Automatically retry whatever operation caused the exception…” option is wrong: there's no basis for assuming a retry would succeed when the cause is an unanticipated bug rather than a transient failure. The “Nothing needs to be done -- Node…” option is wrong: Node doesn't restart anything for you, and a handler that doesn't exit actively prevents the default, safer behavior of crashing.

assessments.prompt: Which of these is the best example of an operational error, as this concept distinguishes it from a programmer error?
options: An off-by-one bug that corrupts an array's contents partway through a loop.
A downstream payment API returning a 503 Service Unavailable during a temporary outage.
A TypeError caused by reading a property off a value that, according to the code's own design, should never have been undefined at that point.
A violated invariant deep in application logic that reveals the program's own internal assumptions about its state were wrong.
assessments.explanation: An operational error is a failure a correctly written program can expect because the outside world is unreliable. A downstream service being temporarily unavailable is a textbook example, and a well-written caller anticipates and handles it (retry, fall back, surface a clean error). The “A TypeError caused by reading a property…”, “An off-by-one bug that corrupts an array's…”, and “A violated invariant deep in application logic…” options all describe programmer errors: bugs showing that the code's own logic or assumptions were wrong, not that the environment failed to cooperate.

assessments.prompt: What is the practical purpose of adding an explicit isOperational flag to a custom error class (such as class AppError extends Error)?
options: It turns an implicit, easy-to-get-wrong judgment call -- 'is this an anticipated failure or an unexpected bug' -- into an explicit, deliberate decision made at the moment the error is created, letting downstream error-handling code decide between a graceful response and a controlled crash based on that flag.
It changes how JavaScript's built-in try/catch mechanism behaves specifically for that error type.
It's required by Node.js itself -- errors created without this flag are silently discarded by the runtime.
It automatically retries whatever operation caused the error, up to a configurable number of attempts.
assessments.explanation: JavaScript's Error type has no concept of 'this was anticipated' versus 'this is a bug'. The isOperational flag is an application-level convention that makes the judgment explicit where the error is constructed, so error-handling middleware (or any centralized handler) can branch on it: a specific, graceful response for operational errors, versus a logged, generic response followed by a controlled exit for anything unmarked. The “It changes how JavaScript's built-in try/catch mechanism…” option is wrong: try/catch behaves identically whatever custom properties the thrown value has. The “It's required by Node.js itself -- errors…” option is wrong: Node has no awareness of this application-defined flag. The “It automatically retries whatever operation caused…” option is wrong: the flag carries no retry behavior and is purely informational.

assessments.prompt: Why does deliberately calling process.exit(1) after logging a genuine programmer error work well as a production strategy, rather than being reckless?
options: Because process.exit() automatically fixes the underlying bug before the next process starts.
Because a crashed process is inherently faster to restart than one that keeps running, regardless of what (if anything) is supervising it.
Because in a typical production deployment, something is actively supervising the process specifically to restart it.
Because Node automatically spawns an internal replacement process whenever process.exit(1) is called, with no external supervision required.
assessments.explanation: The strategy works because production deployments almost always run under something that notices a process exiting and brings up a fresh one quickly; without that supervision a crash would be an outage with no recovery. With it, exiting converts an unknown amount of potential state corruption into a clean, known-good restart, which beats continuing atop possibly corrupted state. The “Because process.exit() automatically fixes the underlying bug…” option is wrong: exiting fixes nothing, it only limits the blast radius. The “Because Node automatically spawns an internal replacement…” option is wrong: Node doesn't spawn replacement processes; that's the job of external supervision. The “Because a crashed process is inherently faster…” option is wrong: the benefit isn't restart speed, it's replacing unknown corrupted state with a clean one, and that disappears without something restarting the process.

assessments.prompt: A teammate argues: 'Our error-handling middleware should catch every error and always respond with a normal-looking JSON error response -- crashing the process is never acceptable in production, no matter what caused the error.' Explain what's right and what's dangerously wrong about this position, using the operational-vs-programmer-error distinction.
assessments.modelAnswer: The instinct is reasonable for one category of errors. An anticipated, operational failure (a user submitting invalid input, a downstream service timing out, a record that doesn't exist) should be caught and turned into a clean, well-formed error response; that's what error-handling middleware and marked operational errors (an isOperational flag on a custom error class, say) are for, and crashing over something that routine would make the service needlessly fragile. The position becomes dangerous when the same 'always respond normally, never crash' policy is extended to errors that were never anticipated: a TypeError from a bug in the code's logic, a violated assumption about the shape of some data, an invariant that broke upstream. Those errors mean the process's model of its own state has diverged from reality in a way the code never accounted for, and by the time the error surfaces there's no reliable way to know how much in-memory state (caches, counters, connection pools, anything mutable) was already affected. Catching that kind of error and responding as if all is well treats an unknown, unbounded problem as a known, bounded one, and the process keeps running with whatever corruption already occurred, until it surfaces as a stranger failure elsewhere. The safer response to an unanticipated error is to log it in full, respond to the one request that triggered it with a generic 500 (not a specific message that assumes you understand what went wrong), and exit, relying on whatever supervises the process in production (pm2, Kubernetes, a container orchestrator, systemd) to bring up a fresh instance almost immediately. That's a controlled, brief failure; treating every error identically in the name of 'never crashing' risks a longer, less visible one.

concepts.title: Debugging Node Applications: --inspect and Beyond console.log
concepts.description: console.log gets you surprisingly far, but it runs out of road when you need to inspect live state, step through execution line by line, or measure something accurately. Node ships a debugger built on the protocol Chrome DevTools speaks, plus a family of console methods most developers never discover, and together they close that gap.
learningObjectives: Explain the specific limitations of console.log-only debugging that motivate reaching for a real debugger.
Start a Node process with --inspect or --inspect-brk and attach a debugging client to set breakpoints and step through code.
Use the debugger statement as an inline breakpoint, and explain when it does and doesn't have any effect.
Use console methods beyond log -- error, warn, table, time/timeEnd, trace, and dir -- for situations plain console.log handles poorly.
Explain the difference between stdout and stderr as it relates to console.log vs console.error, and why that distinction matters for redirected output.

sections.heading: Where console.log Runs Out of Road
sections.body: console.log is a fine first tool for most debugging. It needs no setup, works everywhere, and for a quick 'what value does this variable have right here' question it's often faster than anything more elaborate. Its limits show up once a bug gets moderately tricky. It requires editing code, adding a log statement, and re-running the program for every new piece of information; there's no way to pause execution and look around at what's in scope. It gives a static snapshot at one line, with no way to step forward and watch values change. Deeply nested objects print truncated ([Object]) rather than something you can explore. And it has no way to measure how long something takes, tabulate structured data, or distinguish routine informational output from a problem, short of manual formatting each time. Node's built-in debugger and the other console methods close these gaps.

sections.heading: Attaching a Real Debugger with --inspect
sections.body:
Running node --inspect app.js starts your script as normal but also opens a debugging server (by default on port 9229) that speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, the protocol the browser's DevTools use internally. By default it listens only on 127.0.0.1, which is deliberate: binding the inspector to a public address (--inspect=0.0.0.0:9229) would let anyone who can reach the port run arbitrary code in your process. Any compatible client can attach: open chrome://inspect in Chrome and click 'inspect' next to your process, or use VS Code's built-in Node debugger (via a launch configuration or the 'Attach to Node Process' command). You get a full debugging interface: breakpoints set by clicking a line number, stepping line by line (step over, step into, step out), every variable in scope, live watch expressions, and the full call stack at the point execution is paused.

```bash
node --inspect app.js
# Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/<some-id>
# For help, see: https://nodejs.org/en/docs/inspector
```

node --inspect-brk app.js does the same but also pauses on the first line of your script, before anything else runs, and waits for a debugger client to attach before continuing. That's useful for bugs that happen early in startup, or when you want breakpoints in code that would otherwise run to completion (or crash) before you could attach a client. Compare this with console.log: instead of editing the file and re-running it for every new question, you pause at a breakpoint and inspect, step, and re-inspect anything in scope without touching the source.

sections.heading: The debugger Statement: An Inline Breakpoint
console's Other Methods: Beyond log
sections.body:
console.log has several close relatives, each solving a problem log handles poorly:

- **console.error(...) / console.warn(...)** write to stderr instead of stdout (console.log always writes to stdout). This matters for redirection: `node app.js > output.txt` captures only stdout into output.txt, while anything sent via console.error still appears on the terminal. That lets you separate routine output from problems, or pipe and filter them independently in a shell pipeline or a log aggregation system.
- **console.table(data)** renders an array of objects (or a plain object) as a formatted table in the terminal, which is much easier to scan than a wall of nested console.log output once there are more than a couple of records.
- **console.time(label) / console.timeEnd(label)** bracket a section of code and print the elapsed time between the two calls, which is less fiddly than subtracting two Date.now() values yourself.
- **console.trace(message)** prints the current call stack (which function called which, all the way up) without throwing anything. It answers 'who called this function, and from where' without a breakpoint. (If you prefer a terminal to a GUI, node inspect app.js starts Node's built-in command-line debugger, with commands such as next, step and cont.)
- **console.assert(condition, message)** logs message only if condition is falsy (to stderr, prefixed with 'Assertion failed'), a lightweight way to flag 'this should never happen' situations inline without an if statement. It doesn't throw or stop the program. For a burst of related output, console.group(label) indents everything logged until the matching console.groupEnd(), which keeps the output of one request or one loop iteration visually together.
- **console.dir(obj, { depth: null })** forces full expansion of a deeply nested object, which fixes the '[Object]' truncation plain console.log runs into once nesting passes its default depth of two levels.

```javascript
// fragment: the await below needs an async function (or an ES module) and a `db` client
console.table([{ name: 'Amy', score: 92 }, { name: 'Ben', score: 78 }]);

console.time('db-query');
await db.query('SELECT * FROM orders');
console.timeEnd('db-query');   // logs something like: db-query: 42.318ms

console.dir(deeplyNestedConfig, { depth: null });   // fully expands every level
```

sections.heading: Debugging Isn't Only a Local-Dev Thing
sections.body: You might assume --inspect only applies to a script you're running on your own machine with the source open in an editor, but the inspector can also be enabled on a running process. On POSIX systems, sending a running Node process the SIGUSR1 signal (kill -USR1 <pid>) turns on the inspector without restarting it, which is occasionally useful for investigating a production process without a redeploy. There are security considerations: the inspector grants substantial control over the process, so exposing it outside a tightly controlled network is a real risk, not a convenience to enable casually. For reading stack traces after the fact rather than debugging live, --stack-trace-limit controls how many frames Node prints (the default, 10, is sometimes too shallow to see the origin of a deeply nested async failure), and --trace-warnings prints the full stack trace for deprecation and process warnings that would otherwise print a brief one-line message.

examples.title: Catching an Unexpectedly Undefined Value with --inspect-brk
examples.explanation: The bug, a missing discountRate field on order, produces NaN rather than an error. That quiet, non-crashing failure is hard to track down with console.log alone, since you'd have to guess in advance to log order.discountRate. Running with --inspect-brk and attaching a client pauses at the debugger statement, before the buggy line runs, and lets you inspect the whole order object as it exists at that point and see the missing field, without having predicted which value to log.

examples.title: console.table and console.time for Structured, Measured Output
examples.explanation: console.table(results) renders the array as a grid with columns for endpoint, status, and ms, which scans far better than three console.log(JSON.stringify(...)) calls, especially as the array grows. console.time/console.timeEnd bracket the filtering and report how long it took, with no manual Date.now() subtraction. console.warn (rather than console.log) is used for the summary because it flags something deserving attention and writes to stderr, which matters if this script's output is piped or redirected: a shell script reading results from stdout won't see, or be confused by, this warning line.

examples.title: console.log vs console.error and Stream Redirection
examples.explanation: console.log and console.error write to two separate output streams, stdout and stderr, which the operating system and shell treat as independent channels that can be redirected separately. Redirecting only stdout (> output.txt) captures the routine message in the file but leaves the error message on the terminal, since it never touched stdout. That's why using console.error (or console.warn) for real problems, instead of console.log for everything, matters in practice: whoever runs the process can filter, redirect, or pipe normal output and error output independently, for example sending only errors to a monitoring system while routine logs go to a rotating file. That's impossible if every message goes through console.log.

misconceptions.description: console.log and console.error are functionally identical -- console.error is just a naming convention for 'log statements about errors,' both print to the same place.
misconceptions.clarification: They write to different operating-system-level streams: console.log (and console.info) write to stdout, while console.error (and console.warn) write to stderr. Both appear together, interleaved, when you watch a terminal, which is why the difference is easy to miss. Once either stream is redirected or piped on its own (common in scripts, containers, and log aggregation pipelines), the distinction matters: redirecting stdout to a file captures console.log output but not console.error output, and vice versa.

misconceptions.description: node --inspect only works for debugging a script you're about to run locally -- it can't be used against a process that's already running, especially not in a deployed environment.
misconceptions.clarification: Starting a process with --inspect from the command line is the most common way to use it, but Node's inspector can also be enabled on a running process via the SIGUSR1 signal on POSIX systems (kill -USR1 <pid>), without restarting anything. That makes it possible to attach a debugger to a running production process to investigate a live issue, but it's a security consideration: the inspector grants substantial control over the process, and exposing its port outside a tightly controlled, trusted network is a real risk, not something to enable casually because it's technically possible.

exercises.prompt: Given this script, and the command `node app.js 1> stdout.txt 2> stderr.txt` (redirecting stdout and stderr to two separate files), what ends up in each file?
hints: console.log writes to stdout; console.error and console.warn both write to stderr. Sort each line by the method that produced it.
'1> stdout.txt' redirects file descriptor 1 (stdout); '2> stderr.txt' redirects file descriptor 2 (stderr). They go into two separate files, not merged.
The order lines were logged in doesn't change which stream each belongs to. Group them by console method, not by position in the script.
exercises.expectedAnswer: stdout.txt contains, in order: 'Step 1: starting up', 'Step 2: connected to database', 'Step 3: ready to accept requests'. stderr.txt contains, in order: 'Warning: using default config, none was provided', 'Notice: cache is disabled in this environment'.
exercises.solutionExplanation: console.log writes to stdout (file descriptor 1) and console.error/console.warn write to stderr (file descriptor 2), whatever order they're called in. The three console.log calls ('Step 1', 'Step 2', 'Step 3') go to stdout, and '1> stdout.txt' redirects that stream into stdout.txt, so all three lines land there in the order logged. The console.error and console.warn calls go to stderr, and '2> stderr.txt' redirects that separate stream into stderr.txt, so those two lines end up there, in their original relative order, and are absent from stdout.txt because they were never written to that stream.

exercises.prompt: A developer is trying to debug why a deeply nested configuration object is missing an expected field, but console.log(config) just prints '[Object]' for the nested parts, hiding the actual data. Fix their debugging approach (not the underlying config bug itself) so the real structure is actually visible.
hints: console.log has a default depth limit on how many levels of nested objects it expands before truncating. What happens once you go deeper than that?
console.dir(obj, options) accepts an options object, including a depth setting, that can override the default truncation.
Setting depth to null (rather than a number) tells console.dir to expand every level, however deeply nested.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Plain console.log(config) uses util.inspect's default depth (2), which stops expanding nested objects after that many levels and prints [Object] for anything deeper, the truncation this developer hit because tls.options is nested three levels down. console.dir(config, { depth: null }) uses the same inspection mechanism but overrides depth to null, which removes the limit and prints every level, revealing the hidden tls.options.minVersion without logging fields individually by name (which would require already knowing where to look).

assessments.prompt: What is the specific difference between running `node --inspect app.js` and `node --inspect-brk app.js`?
options: --inspect starts the script running immediately and opens a debugger port for a client to attach to whenever it's ready; --inspect-brk does the same, but additionally pauses execution on the very first line, waiting for a client to attach before running anything else.
--inspect-brk permanently disables console.log output in favor of the debugger's own logging panel.
--inspect only works with Chrome DevTools, while --inspect-brk only works with VS Code's debugger.
--inspect-brk is simply a faster version of --inspect with no functional difference in behavior.
assessments.explanation: Both flags open the same Chrome DevTools Protocol debugging server; the difference is timing. --inspect lets the script start running right away, and a client can attach later to set breakpoints from then on (missing anything that already ran). --inspect-brk also pauses execution on the first line until a debugging client attaches, which helps catch bugs in code that runs very early, before you could otherwise attach anything. The “--inspect-brk is simply a faster version…” option ignores a real behavioral difference. The “--inspect only works with Chrome DevTools, while…” option is wrong: both flags work with any client that speaks the protocol, including Chrome DevTools and VS Code. The “--inspect-brk permanently disables console.log output in favor…” option is wrong: console.log works normally alongside the debugger.

assessments.prompt: A codebase has a `debugger;` statement left inside a function, and the app is run in production via a plain `node app.js`, with no --inspect flag and no debugging client ever attached. What happens when execution reaches that line?
options: Node throws a ReferenceError, since debugger is not a valid statement outside of an active debugging session.
The process pauses indefinitely, waiting for a debugger client that will never attach, effectively hanging forever.
It automatically starts an --inspect-style debugging server on the spot, opening port 9229 for a client to attach to.
It's a complete no-op -- execution continues past it exactly as if it were a comment.
assessments.explanation: The debugger statement's behavior depends on whether a debugging client is attached when execution reaches it. With no client (an ordinary node app.js run), it has no effect, like a comment. That makes it reasonably safe to leave in temporarily while debugging, though it should be removed before committing. The “The process pauses indefinitely, waiting…” option confuses it with a breakpoint set via an attached client; without a client, there's nothing to pause for. The “Node throws a ReferenceError, since debugger…” option is wrong: debugger is standard JavaScript syntax whatever the debugging state. The “It automatically starts an --inspect-style debugging server…” option is wrong: reaching a debugger statement never starts an inspector server; that needs the --inspect flag at startup.

assessments.prompt: A script runs console.log('started') followed by console.error('config missing, using defaults'). It's launched as `node app.js > output.txt`, redirecting only stdout. What ends up in output.txt?
options: Both lines -- 'started' and 'config missing, using defaults'.
Only 'started' -- console.error writes to stderr, a stream separate from stdout, so redirecting stdout alone does not capture it.
Only 'config missing, using defaults', since console.error output takes precedence over console.log when both are present in a redirected run.
Neither line -- redirecting stdout with a single > suppresses all console output entirely, from any method.
assessments.explanation: console.log and console.error write to two separate OS-level streams, stdout and stderr. `> output.txt` redirects only stdout, so only the console.log line ends up in the file; the console.error line still goes to stderr, which here is unredirected and prints to the terminal. The “Both lines -- 'started' and 'config missing, using defaults'” option wrongly assumes both streams are captured together. The “Only 'config missing, using defaults', since console.error…” option invents a precedence rule; the streams operate independently. The “Neither line -- redirecting stdout…” option is wrong: redirection affects only the stream being redirected.

assessments.prompt: A developer wants to (1) measure the precise elapsed time of an async database call without manually subtracting two Date.now() timestamps, and (2) render an array of result objects as an easily scannable grid instead of a wall of nested console output. Which console methods directly address these two needs, respectively?
options: console.dir (for timing) and console.warn (for tabular data).
console.trace (for timing) and console.assert (for tabular data).
console.time/console.timeEnd (bracketing a section of code to report precise elapsed duration) and console.table (rendering an array of objects as a formatted, scannable table).
console.group (for timing) and console.count (for tabular data).
assessments.explanation: console.time(label)/console.timeEnd(label) bracket a section of code and print the elapsed time between the two calls, replacing the manual Date.now() subtraction you'd otherwise do. console.table(data) renders an array of objects as a grid in the terminal, much easier to scan than repeated nested console.log calls. None of the methods in the other options address either need: console.trace prints a call stack, console.assert conditionally logs a message, console.dir controls object-expansion depth, console.warn is a stderr-writing variant of log, console.group indents related log lines, and console.count tracks how many times a labeled line was logged. None measure elapsed time or render tabular data.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer who only ever uses console.log when and why they should reach for --inspect and a real debugger instead, and mention at least two other console methods worth knowing that solve problems console.log handles poorly.
assessments.modelAnswer: console.log is a fine starting point for simple questions ('what value does this variable have right here, right now'), and for those, anything heavier is unnecessary overhead. It stops being enough when a bug requires exploring state you didn't think to log in advance, watching how several values change across steps rather than at one line, or inspecting a deeply nested object that console.log truncates into [Object]. Each of those means editing the source and re-running the program to add one more piece of visibility, which gets slow once a bug takes more than a couple of guesses. Running the process with node --inspect (or --inspect-brk, which also pauses on the first line before anything else runs) opens a debugging server that a client like Chrome DevTools or VS Code's debugger can attach to. You set breakpoints by clicking a line number, pause there, inspect every variable in scope, step forward line by line to watch values change, and view the full call stack, all without editing the source and without having predicted which values you'd need. Two console methods are worth knowing because console.log handles their use cases poorly: console.dir(obj, { depth: null }) fully expands a deeply nested object instead of truncating into [Object] past the default depth, and console.table(arrayOfObjects) renders repetitive structured data (like a list of records) as a formatted table, far easier to scan than a stack of logged objects. A third is console.time(label)/console.timeEnd(label), which brackets a section of code and reports the elapsed time, sparing you from subtracting two Date.now() timestamps each time you measure something. None of these replace console.log; each fills one gap it leaves.
